target: शोभा बीमार थी तो दफ़्तर नहीं गई।
english: Shobha was sick, so she did not go to the office.
tip: तो (to) after a whole clause means 'so': बीमार थी तो (beemaar thi to = she was sick, so...). No separate word for 'so' is needed.

target: मौसम तो ख़राब था, पर ट्रिप मज़ेदार रही।
english: The weather was bad, but the trip was fun.
tip: तो (to) right after a word concedes it: मौसम तो ख़राब था (mausam to kharaab tha) = 'the weather WAS bad, sure' – and a पर (par = but) is coming.

target: नीता अनुभवी है, इसीलिए यह काम उसी को मिला।
english: Neeta is experienced, which is exactly why this work went to her.
tip: इसीलिए (isiliye) packs ही (hi = exactly) inside इसलिए (isliye = that's why): 'that's precisely why'. उसी को (usi ko) does the same – to her and no one else.

target: वरना निशा को बड़ा नुक़सान हो जाता।
english: Otherwise Nisha would have suffered a big loss.
tip: वरना (varna = otherwise) flips to would-have mode: हो जाता (ho jaata) = would have happened. The bare -ता form carries the whole 'would have'.

target: हालाँकि टिकट महँगे थे, फिर भी हमने फ़िल्म देखी।
english: Although the tickets were expensive, we still watched the movie.
tip: हालाँकि (haalaanki = although) demands an answer in clause two: फिर भी (phir bhi = even so). Dropping the फिर भी sounds unfinished to Hindi ears.

target: मैंने कल के लिए डॉक्टर से मिलने का समय तय कर लिया।
english: I've fixed a time to see the doctor for tomorrow.
tip: Hindi meets 'from' people: डॉक्टर से मिलने (doctor se milne) = to meet the doctor. मिलना (milna = meet) takes से (se = from), never a word for 'with'.

target: दीदी, बहुत दिन हो गए बात किए।
english: Sister, it's been many days since we talked.
tip: बहुत दिन हो गए (bahut din ho gaye) is literally 'many days have become' – Hindi states elapsed time as days happening, with no 'it's been' or 'since'.

target: स्वाति हमेशा दूसरों की मदद करती है।
english: Swati always helps others.
tip: Hindi does someone's help: दूसरों की मदद (doosron ki madad = help of others). मदद करना (madad karna) takes की (ki) – you do the help OF a person, not 'help' them directly.

target: प्रिया को दूसरों की मदद करना अच्छा लगता है।
english: Priya likes helping others.
tip: Liking flips in Hindi: प्रिया को (Priya ko = to Priya) plus अच्छा लगता है (achchha lagta hai = feels good). The liker takes को; the thing liked – helping others – is the subject.

target: जाने से पहले फ़ोन रिचार्ज कर लो।
english: Recharge your phone before leaving.
tip: कर लो (kar lo) is more than plain 'do': लो from लेना (lena = take) adds 'for your own benefit, get it done' – recharge the phone for yourself before leaving.

target: ट्रेन लेट होने की वजह से हमें बहुत देर इंतज़ार करना पड़ा।
english: Because the train was late, we had to wait a long time.
tip: इंतज़ार करना पड़ा (intazaar karna pada) = 'waiting fell on us'. 'Had to' uses पड़ना (padna = fall) – obligation drops on you, so the person takes हमें (hamen = to us).

target: दुकान आठ बजे बंद हो जाती है।
english: The shop closes at eight.
tip: The shop 'goes closed': बंद हो जाती है (band ho jaati hai). जाना (jaana = go) marks a change of state – हो जाना means 'becomes', not just 'is'.

target: माँ ने पूछा कि बच्चे कहाँ गए।
english: Mother asked where the children went.
tip: Hindi keeps कि (ki = that) even before reported questions: पूछा कि बच्चे कहाँ गए (poochha ki bachche kahaan gaye) – literally 'asked that where the children went'.

target: सुरेश ने जवाब दिया कि कल आएगा।
english: Suresh replied that he will come tomorrow.
tip: English shifts to 'he would come' when reporting – Hindi keeps the speaker's original tense: कि कल आएगा (ki kal aayega = that he'll come tomorrow), exactly as Suresh said it.

target: नरेश ने पूछा कि क्या मीटिंग रद्द हुई है।
english: Naresh asked whether the meeting was cancelled.
tip: क्या (kya) usually asks 'what', but right after कि it means 'whether': पूछा कि क्या मीटिंग रद्द हुई है (poochha ki kya meeting radd hui hai = asked whether the meeting was cancelled).

target: विजय बोला, 'मैं तो ज़रूर आऊँगा।'
english: Vijay said, 'I'll definitely come.'
tip: बोलना (bolna = to say) takes no ने (ne) in the past: विजय बोला (Vijay bola). With its synonym कहना (kahna) you'd need ने: विजय ने कहा (Vijay ne kaha) – same meaning, opposite rule.

target: सुनीता को लगा कि कल छुट्टी रहेगी।
english: Sunita thought there would be a holiday tomorrow.
tip: Thoughts land on you in Hindi: सुनीता को लगा (Sunita ko laga = it struck Sunita). She's the receiver of the thought, not the doer – को लगा (ko laga) covers hunches and impressions.

target: कविता का मानना है कि शिक्षा सबसे ज़रूरी है।
english: Kavita believes that education is the most important.
tip: Hindi phrases believing as possession: कविता का मानना है (Kavita ka maanna hai) = literally 'Kavita's believing is'. का (ka = 's) marks the opinion as something she owns.

target: दिव्या के हिसाब से यह योजना कामयाब होगी।
english: According to Divya, this plan will succeed.
tip: 'According to' is literally 'by the calculation of': दिव्या के हिसाब से (Divya ke hisaab se = by Divya's reckoning). के हिसाब से (ke hisaab se) works for anyone's opinion or estimate.

target: मैंने उसे याद दिलाया कि दवा समय पर लेनी है।
english: I reminded him to take the medicine on time.
tip: 'Remind' is याद दिलाना (yaad dilana = cause to get the memory): मैंने उसे याद दिलाया (maine use yaad dilaya = I made him remember). Plain remembering is याद आना (yaad aana = memory comes).

target: भूख के मारे पेट में चूहे कूद रहे हैं।
english: I'm so hungry my stomach is growling.
tip: पेट में चूहे कूद रहे हैं (pet mein choohe kood rahe hain) = 'mice are jumping in my stomach'. English stomachs growl with hunger – Hindi ones fill with jumping mice.

target: कुणाल आज सातवें आसमान पर है।
english: Kunal is on cloud nine today (lit. seventh sky).
tip: सातवें आसमान पर (saatven aasmaan par) = 'on the seventh sky'. Hindi puts extreme happiness up in the sky too – but counts to seven where English's cloud nine counts to nine.

target: जब पुलिस आई तो चोर नौ दो ग्यारह हो गया।
english: When the police came, the thief ran away quickly.
tip: नौ दो ग्यारह हो गया (nau do gyaarah ho gaya) = literally 'became nine-two-eleven', Hindi's stock idiom for bolting. The चोर (chor = thief) vanishes as the police arrive.

target: अनीता अपने माता-पिता की आँखों का तारा है।
english: Anita is the apple of her parents' eyes.
tip: आँखों का तारा (aankhon ka taara) = 'the star of the eyes'. English treasures the apple of the eye – Hindi makes the loved one a तारा (taara = star) instead.

target: दाल में कुछ काला था, बात संदिग्ध लगी।
english: There was something dark in the matter; it seemed suspicious.
tip: दाल में कुछ काला (daal mein kuchh kaala) = 'something black in the dal'. Where English smells something fishy, Hindi spots a dark speck in the lentils – the matter looks suspicious.

target: आजकल मेरा हाथ तंग है।
english: Money's tight for me these days.
tip: हाथ तंग है (haath tang hai) = 'the hand is tight'. When money runs short in Hindi, it's your हाथ (haath = hand) that tightens, not your budget.

target: चरणस्पर्श माता जी।
english: I touch your feet, mother.
tip: चरणस्पर्श (charan-sparsh) is literally 'foot-touch' – a greeting for elders. You can say it without bending down, even on the phone: the word alone carries the respect.

target: ख़ुश आमदीद, तशरीफ़ रखिए।
english: Welcome, please be seated.
tip: तशरीफ़ रखिए (tashreef rakhiye) is literally 'place your honor' – ultra-courteous Urdu-flavored 'please sit'. The guest's honor takes the seat, not the guest.

target: क्या आपके भाई-बहन हैं?
english: Do you have any brothers or sisters?
tip: Hindi has no verb for 'have'. आपके भाई-बहन हैं (aapke bhai-behen hain) is literally 'your brothers-sisters are?' – what you 'have' simply exists as yours.

target: नमस्ते, खाना खाया आपने?
english: Hello, did you eat?
tip: खाना खाया आपने? (khana khaya aapne = did you eat?) works as a warm hello, like 'how are you?' – it signals care, not curiosity about your actual meal.
